title: Lamotrigine and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink on Lamictal?
excerpt: Can you drink on lamotrigine (Lamictal)? How alcohol affects dizziness, seizure risk, and mood on lamotrigine, what to do about missed doses, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on lamotrigine (Lamictal)? How alcohol affects dizziness, seizure risk, and bipolar mood, plus missed-dose and rash safety tips.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** lamotrigine (brand name Lamictal) doesn't have a strong, well-known chemical interaction with alcohol, so a drink isn't expected to push your lamotrigine levels up or down. That's the good news, and it's why many prescribers allow occasional light drinking once your dose is stable. The real risks come from overlap and from what alcohol does to the conditions lamotrigine treats. Both cause dizziness, unsteadiness, sleepiness, and blurred or double vision, so together they hit harder. Heavy drinking can make seizures more likely, especially the next day. And alcohol tends to worsen depression and mood swings in bipolar disorder, which is exactly what lamotrigine is trying to hold steady.

**The quick rules:** Ask your prescriber whether drinking is okay for you, and how much. Never skip or delay a lamotrigine dose because you plan to drink. Avoid alcohol during the first weeks of treatment and after any dose increase, when side effects are strongest. If you do drink, keep it to one or two, have food, go slowly, and don't drive. Protect your sleep, because sleep loss plus alcohol is a classic seizure trigger.

> **This is not medical advice. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on lamotrigine.** This article explains general research and label information. It isn't a substitute for a prescriber who knows your diagnosis, dose, and other medicines. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if** you or someone else has a seizure lasting more than five minutes, repeated seizures without waking up in between, trouble breathing, or can't be woken. **Contact a doctor urgently if** you develop any new rash, blisters, mouth sores, fever, or swollen glands on lamotrigine, or if you have thoughts of harming yourself (in the US you can call or text **988**, the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, any time).

## What Lamotrigine Is and Why People Take It

Lamotrigine is an anti-seizure medicine. It's prescribed for two main reasons:

- **Epilepsy.** It's used on its own or with other anti-seizure drugs for several seizure types in adults and children.
- **Bipolar I disorder.** It's approved for long-term maintenance, meaning it helps delay new mood episodes, and it's especially valued for preventing the depressive side of bipolar disorder. It isn't used to treat an acute manic episode.

Doctors also sometimes prescribe it off-label for other conditions, so you may be taking it for a reason not listed here.

Lamotrigine works mainly by calming overactive nerve signaling. It blocks certain sodium channels on nerve cells and reduces the release of glutamate, the brain's main "go" chemical. In plain terms, it makes nerve cells less likely to fire in the runaway bursts that cause seizures, and that same steadying effect seems to help with mood.

Two things about lamotrigine matter a lot for this topic:

1. **It's started slowly on purpose.** Lamotrigine carries an FDA boxed warning about serious skin rashes, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome. The risk is higher when the dose is started too high or raised too fast, so prescribers build it up over several weeks.
2. **It's long-acting.** Its half-life (the time it takes your body to clear half of a dose) is roughly a day or more in adults, and it changes a lot depending on your other medicines. Valproate roughly doubles it; some older anti-seizure drugs and estrogen-containing birth control speed its clearance. Either way, it's in your system around the clock.

## Lamotrigine and Alcohol: How They Actually Interact

People often expect a dramatic chemical clash, like the one between acetaminophen and alcohol in the liver. That's not really the story with lamotrigine.

**No major chemical interaction.** Lamotrigine is broken down in the liver mainly by a process called glucuronidation (attaching a sugar-like molecule so it can be flushed out), not by the CYP enzymes that alcohol is famous for ramping up. The official prescribing information doesn't list alcohol as something that changes lamotrigine levels. So a drink isn't expected to make your lamotrigine stronger or weaker in your blood.

**But the effects add up.** The interaction that matters is about how you feel and function. Lamotrigine's most common side effects include dizziness, problems with balance and coordination (ataxia), sleepiness, headache, double vision, blurred vision, and nausea. Alcohol causes nearly the same list. When you put them together, you get more of each. That's why many people on lamotrigine report getting tipsy faster, feeling woozier, or seeing double after fewer drinks than they used to.

**And alcohol works against the condition.** For epilepsy, heavy drinking and the hours after it can lower the seizure threshold. For bipolar disorder, alcohol disrupts sleep and mood and is linked to more frequent and harder-to-treat episodes. Lamotrigine can only do so much if alcohol is pushing in the other direction.

## Lamictal and Alcohol: Is the Brand Any Different?

No. Lamictal is the original brand name for lamotrigine, and everything in this guide applies to it, to generic lamotrigine, and to the extended-release (Lamictal XR), chewable, and orally disintegrating versions. The active drug is the same, so the alcohol concerns are the same.

One small practical note: the extended-release versions release the drug more evenly through the day. That doesn't make drinking safer, but it's another reason dose timing isn't a useful way to "work around" alcohol.

## Can You Drink on Lamotrigine? A Practical Framework

There's no universal answer, because the right call depends on why you take it, how stable you are, and what else you take. Here is how the decision usually breaks down. Use it to prepare for a conversation with your prescriber, not to replace one.

**Situations where most prescribers advise avoiding alcohol:**

- You've just started lamotrigine or recently had a dose increase. Side effects like dizziness and double vision are strongest in this phase, and you don't yet know how the drug affects you.
- Your seizures aren't well controlled, or you've had a seizure recently.
- You have bipolar disorder and you're currently depressed, unstable, or have had thoughts of self-harm.
- You also take other sedating medicines, such as benzodiazepines, sleep aids, opioids, gabapentin, or some antipsychotics.
- You've had seizures related to alcohol in the past.

**Situations where a prescriber may say occasional light drinking is okay:**

- You've been on a stable dose for a while with good seizure or mood control.
- You don't take other sedating medicines.
- You know how lamotrigine affects you and side effects are mild.

Even then, the limit is your prescriber's call, not a number from the internet, and "okay" never means a night out. If you haven't asked, the safer default is not to drink until you do.

## Dizziness, Double Vision, and Coordination: The Most Common Problem

For most people, the first thing they notice when drinking on lamotrigine is how unsteady they feel. This deserves its own section because it's the most common real-world issue and the easiest to underestimate.

Lamotrigine's balance and vision side effects are dose-related and are usually worst after starting or raising the dose. Alcohol impairs the same systems: the cerebellum (the part of the brain that handles coordination) and the eye movements that keep your vision single and sharp. Together, the effects stack.

What that looks like in practice:

- Feeling drunk after one or two drinks
- Swaying, stumbling, or misjudging steps and curbs
- Double or blurry vision, especially when you look to the side
- Feeling spaced out or unusually sleepy

**What to do if it happens:** stop drinking, sit or lie down somewhere safe, have water and some food, and let someone know how you feel. Don't drive, cycle, swim, or climb, and don't take anything extra to "sober up." Falls are a genuine risk here, and a fall can also be confused with, or trigger, other problems.

**When it's more than side effects:** severe double vision that doesn't settle, being unable to walk, confusion, or vomiting repeatedly needs medical attention. If you're on lamotrigine and also take valproate, your lamotrigine levels run higher than usual, which can make these effects stronger.

## Alcohol, Seizures, and the Seizure Threshold

If you take lamotrigine for epilepsy, this is the most important section.

Your "seizure threshold" is how much it takes to set off a seizure. Lamotrigine raises that threshold. Alcohol affects it in two phases:

1. **While you're drinking,** alcohol acts as a depressant on the brain. Small amounts aren't known to trigger seizures in most people with well-controlled epilepsy.
2. **As alcohol wears off,** the brain rebounds into a more excitable state. This is why alcohol-related seizures often happen the morning after or later the next day, not during the night out. The heavier the drinking, the bigger the rebound. (If you want more on why alcohol behaves this way, see our explainer on [whether alcohol is a depressant](/never-hungover/is-alcohol-a-depressant).)

Several things that tend to come with a night of drinking also make seizures more likely on their own:

- **Missed or late doses.** Forgetting your evening lamotrigine after a night out is one of the most common ways drinking leads to a seizure.
- **Sleep deprivation.** Late nights and alcohol-disrupted sleep are well-known seizure triggers.
- **Vomiting.** If you throw up shortly after taking a dose, you may not absorb all of it. Ask your pharmacist what to do in that case rather than guessing.
- **Dehydration and skipped meals.**

**Practical steps if your doctor says light drinking is okay:**

- Take your lamotrigine on schedule, every time. Set an alarm if your evening plans run late.
- Stay within the limit your prescriber set, spaced out, with food.
- Get a full night's sleep afterward.
- Tell the people you're with that you have epilepsy and what to do if you have a seizure.
- Avoid binge drinking completely. It's the pattern most clearly tied to seizures.

**Important:** if you drink heavily most days, don't suddenly stop on your own. Stopping alcohol abruptly after regular heavy use can cause withdrawal, which can include seizures. Talk to a doctor about a safe plan.

## Alcohol, Mood, and Bipolar Disorder

If you take lamotrigine for bipolar disorder, alcohol's main risk isn't chemical. It's what alcohol does to mood and sleep.

- **Alcohol is a depressant.** It may lift your mood briefly, but the next day often brings low mood, irritability, and anxiety. For someone whose medicine is meant to prevent depressive episodes, that's working against the treatment.
- **It disrupts sleep.** Alcohol fragments sleep in the second half of the night. Sleep disruption is one of the most reliable triggers for mood episodes in bipolar disorder, in both directions.
- **It can blunt judgment.** That matters more when mood is already shifting.
- **It's harder to tell what's causing what.** If you drink regularly, it becomes hard for you and your doctor to know whether low mood is the illness, the alcohol, or the medicine not working.

All anti-seizure medicines, lamotrigine included, carry an FDA warning about a small increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behavior. Alcohol can intensify low mood and lower inhibitions. If you notice worsening depression, new or stronger thoughts of self-harm, or unusual changes in behavior, tell your doctor promptly. If you're in crisis, call or text **988** in the US, or call 911.

The day-after anxiety many people feel after drinking (sometimes called "hangxiety") can feel especially sharp if you're prone to mood symptoms. Our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) explains why it happens.

## Missed Doses, Restarting, and the Rash Warning

Alcohol doesn't cause the serious lamotrigine rash, and there's no good evidence linking the two directly. But there's an indirect connection worth knowing about, because it's a safety issue specific to this drug.

The lamotrigine label says that if you stop taking it for a significant period (the label uses a period based on the drug's half-life, which works out to several days for many people), you may need to restart at a low dose and build up again, rather than going straight back to your old dose. Restarting at a full dose after a break raises the risk of a serious rash.

So the risk pattern to avoid is this: a heavy weekend or a stretch of drinking leads to missed doses for several days, then you restart at your usual dose. If that happens, **don't restart on your own. Call your prescriber or pharmacist first** and ask how to resume.

For a single missed dose, follow your own prescriber's instructions. In general, the advice is to take it when you remember unless it's almost time for your next dose, and never to double up.

**Rash warning signs that need urgent care:** any new rash, especially with fever, blisters, peeling skin, mouth or eye sores, swollen glands, or feeling generally unwell. Most rashes on lamotrigine are not serious, but you can't tell which ones are by looking, so get it checked the same day.

## Other Medicines That Change the Picture

Many people on lamotrigine take other medicines too. Some of them make alcohol riskier:

- **Valproate (Depakote).** Raises lamotrigine levels, often meaning stronger dizziness and coordination effects. Valproate also has its own liver warnings, which matters if you drink.
- **Carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital.** Lower lamotrigine levels and are sedating on their own. Carbamazepine commonly causes dizziness, which stacks with alcohol.
- **Benzodiazepines (like clonazepam or lorazepam), sleep aids, and opioids.** These are the most concerning, because combined with alcohol they can slow breathing. See our guide on [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) for why that combination is dangerous.
- **Gabapentin or pregabalin.** Sometimes used alongside lamotrigine; they add sedation and dizziness. Our [gabapentin and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) covers this.
- **Antidepressants and antipsychotics.** Common in bipolar treatment, and several add sleepiness. If you take an SSRI, our [Lexapro and alcohol](/never-hungover/lexapro-and-alcohol) guide covers the mood side.
- **Estrogen-containing birth control.** Doesn't involve alcohol, but it lowers lamotrigine levels and can affect seizure or mood control, so mention it to your prescriber.

The FDA also issued a safety communication in 2021 noting that lamotrigine may affect heart rhythm in people with certain existing heart conditions. If you have a known heart problem and notice a racing or irregular heartbeat, fainting, or chest pain, after drinking or at any time, get medical advice promptly.

For a broader look at how supplements and medicines can interact, see our [medication interactions safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## Hangovers on Lamotrigine

Hangovers can feel worse on lamotrigine, for a few reasons. Both alcohol and lamotrigine can cause headache, nausea, dizziness, and grogginess, and a hangover is when the brain's rebound excitability is highest, which is a concern for anyone with epilepsy.

If you wake up hungover:

- **Take your morning dose on time** if that's your schedule. Don't skip it because you feel rough.
- **Drink water and eat** something simple.
- **Rest,** and plan for an early night to recover lost sleep.
- **Be careful with pain relievers.** Ask your pharmacist which one is right for you given your other medicines. Avoid combination "nighttime" products that add sleep aids.
- **Don't drive** if you're still dizzy, unsteady, or seeing double.
- **Watch for warning signs.** Unusual muscle jerks, staring spells, or the aura you sometimes get before a seizure should be treated seriously. Contact your doctor, and call 911 for a seizure lasting more than five minutes.

## How Long After Lamotrigine Can You Drink?

There isn't a safe gap, because lamotrigine is a daily medicine with a long half-life. If you take it every day, it never fully clears between doses, so you can't time a drink to avoid the overlap. Skipping a dose to make room for drinking is a bad idea: it lowers your protection against seizures or mood episodes, and missing several doses creates the restarting problem described above.

If you've stopped lamotrigine completely under medical supervision, it usually takes several days to a week or more to clear, depending on your other medicines. Your pharmacist can give you a more specific answer.

## A Note on DHM and Lamotrigine

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that some people take around drinking. Research, mostly in animals, suggests it may support how the body handles alcohol and may act on the brain's GABA-A calming system. Human data are limited, and there's no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in everyone.

**There's no research on DHM combined with lamotrigine.** Because DHM appears to affect brain signaling, and lamotrigine is an anti-seizure and mood-stabilizing medicine, ask your doctor or pharmacist before combining them. DHM does not make it safe to drink on lamotrigine, doesn't protect against seizures, and doesn't change any of the advice above.

If your prescriber is comfortable with you using it, think of DHM as a modest helper for occasional, light social drinking, not a safety net. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts, and our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the basics that matter more than any supplement: pacing, food, water, and sleep.

## The Bottom Line

Lamotrigine and alcohol don't have a major chemical interaction, but that doesn't make the combination risk-free. The practical dangers are stronger dizziness and double vision, a higher chance of seizures after heavy drinking or a missed dose, and worse mood and sleep for people with bipolar disorder. If your prescriber says light drinking is okay, stay within the limit they set, drink with food, never skip a dose, protect your sleep, and don't drive. If you've missed several days of lamotrigine, call your prescriber before restarting.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking lamotrigine (Lamictal)?**

Lamotrigine has no well-known chemical interaction with alcohol, so a single drink is not expected to change your lamotrigine levels. The concerns are different: both cause dizziness, unsteadiness, sleepiness, and blurred or double vision, and heavy drinking can lower the seizure threshold and destabilize mood. Many prescribers are fine with occasional light drinking once your dose is stable, but that is a decision to make with your own doctor.

**Does alcohol make lamotrigine less effective?**

Alcohol does not appear to break down lamotrigine faster the way some drugs do, so it is unlikely to lower your blood levels directly. It can still undo the benefit indirectly. Heavy drinking, hangovers, poor sleep, and missed doses all make seizures more likely, and alcohol can worsen depression and mood swings in bipolar disorder, which are the very things lamotrigine is meant to prevent.

**Can drinking on lamotrigine cause a seizure?**

Light drinking is not known to trigger seizures in most people with well-controlled epilepsy, but heavy drinking can. The risk is often highest the next day, as alcohol wears off and the brain rebounds, especially if you also slept badly or missed a dose. If you have epilepsy, never skip lamotrigine because you plan to drink, and ask your neurologist what limit is safe for you.

**Why do I feel so dizzy when I drink on Lamictal?**

Dizziness, poor coordination, and blurred or double vision are among the most common lamotrigine side effects, and alcohol causes the same effects. Together they add up, so one or two drinks can hit harder than you expect, particularly soon after a dose increase. Sit down, stop drinking, drink water, and do not drive. If you have severe double vision, cannot walk, or are confused, get medical help.

**What should I do if I miss lamotrigine doses because of drinking?**

If you miss a single dose, follow your prescriber's or pharmacist's instructions, which usually means taking it when you remember unless it is nearly time for the next one. Do not double up. If you have missed several days in a row, do not simply restart your usual dose. The label says people who stop for a significant period may need to restart at a low dose and build up again, because restarting at a full dose raises the risk of a serious rash. Call your prescriber first.

**How long after taking lamotrigine can I drink?**

There is no waiting period that makes it safe, because lamotrigine is taken every day and its half-life is roughly a day or more, so it is always in your system. Timing a drink around your dose does not avoid the overlap. The more useful questions for your doctor are how much, if any, is reasonable for you, and how to protect your sleep and your dose schedule.

**Can alcohol cause the Lamictal rash?**

There is no good evidence that alcohol itself causes the serious lamotrigine rash. The main known risk factors are starting too high, increasing too fast, taking it with valproate, and restarting at full dose after a break. Drinking matters only if it leads to missed doses or a stop-and-restart pattern. Any new rash on lamotrigine, especially with fever, blisters, mouth sores, or swollen glands, needs urgent medical attention.

**Can I take DHM while on lamotrigine?**

There is no good evidence on how DHM and lamotrigine interact, because the combination has not been studied in people. DHM appears to act on the brain's GABA calming system in animal research, so ask your doctor or pharmacist before combining it with an anti-seizure or mood-stabilizing medicine. DHM does not make drinking safe on lamotrigine and is not a substitute for your prescriber's advice.
